story.title: Voting Begins in Russia's Wartime Parliamentary Election
story.summary: Russians have commenced three days of voting in the country's first parliamentary election held during wartime. The election is characterized by a lack of opposition, which is expected to reinforce the Kremlin's political control.

timeline_highlights.title: Russians Vote in Parliamentary Elections Amid Ongoing War and Limited Opposition
timeline_highlights.summary: Russians are participating in a three-day parliamentary election, the first since the invasion of Ukraine, where only pro-Kremlin parties are on the ballot. The elections are viewed by many as a means for the Kremlin to reinforce its power and legitimacy, with fears of mobilization overshadowing the voting process. Most anti-war candidates have been excluded, raising concerns about the authenticity of the electoral process.

event_overview.title: About Russia Elections
event_overview.subject: Russia Elections
event_overview.summary: Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election chooses the ninth convocation of the State Duma, the elected lower chamber of the Federal Assembly. Voting is being held during Russia’s war against Ukraine and alongside regional and municipal elections; the political environment has been marked by restrictions on opposition activity.

facts.label: Voting period
facts.value: Voting for the 2026 State Duma election is scheduled across three days, September 18–20, 2026; September 20 is the single voting day.

facts.label: Institution being elected
facts.value: The State Duma is the lower chamber of Russia’s Federal Assembly (parliament) and has 450 deputies.

facts.label: Electoral system
facts.value: The election uses a mixed system: 225 deputies are elected in single-member districts and 225 from federal party lists in proportional representation.

facts.label: Term and election authority
facts.value: State Duma deputies serve five-year terms. Under the federal election law, the president calls regular Duma elections, while election commissions administer the process under election legislation.

facts.label: Voter and candidate eligibility
facts.value: Russian citizens aged 18 or older may vote; a candidate for the State Duma must be at least 21 and permanently reside in Russia, subject to other legal qualifications and restrictions.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected timeline covers the opening of voting on September 18, 2026, rather than the full campaign, regional contests, vote count, certification, or longer-term political consequences.

explore_lenses.label: What changed for anti-war voters?
explore_lenses.title: Yabloko lost its nationwide party-list ballot
explore_lenses.summary: The principal change was the removal of Yabloko's federal candidate list shortly before voting. That leaves anti-war voters without a registered anti-war party list, although Yabloko candidates remain in some single-member district races.

claims.text: Russia's Supreme Court cancelled registration of Yabloko's federal list on August 10; its August 17 appellate ruling left that decision in place.

The court said the case concerned alleged copyright violations in campaign material and funds received from people who had themselves received foreign-state financing; it said extremism allegations were outside this case.
Yabloko co-founder Grigory Yavlinsky called the exclusion a refusal to engage people raising uncomfortable questions and said the party wanted peace, freedom and life without fear.
AP reports that Yabloko is off the party-list ballot but still has candidates in single-seat contests; the other nine registered parties support President Vladimir Putin's policies.

explore_lenses.label: Who is voting in occupied Ukrainian areas?
explore_lenses.title: The electorate now includes four Russian-claimed regions
explore_lenses.summary: Russia has extended the Duma vote into Ukrainian territory it occupies and claims to have annexed. Moscow treats those residents as part of its electorate; Ukraine rejects both the voting and any resulting mandates.

claims.text: For the first time in a Russian parliamentary election, the electorate includes residents of four Ukrainian regions seized by Russia after 2022; voting is also occurring in Crimea.
Russia's Central Election Commission adopted special rules for conducting the Duma election under martial law in parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry says voting organized by Russia in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory is illegal and void, and says it will not recognize results, election commissions or mandates arising from it.

Ukraine's sanctions-policy commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said people organizing the elections in occupied territory would face sanctions; that is a stated policy intention, not a documented completed sanction action as of September 18.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the three voting days?
explore_lenses.title: Votes will determine all 450 Duma seats
explore_lenses.summary: Voting runs September 18-20, after which Russia's election authorities will count separate party-list and constituency ballots. The election combines national party representation with district contests rather than using a single nationwide ballot alone.

claims.text: The Central Election Commission scheduled voting for September 18, 19 and 20, 2026; its resolution also provides special early-day arrangements for certain remote locations and some voters abroad.
All 450 State Duma seats are at stake: 225 are allocated through party lists and 225 through single-member constituencies, with voters casting two ballots.
The Central Election Commission authorized remote electronic voting in specified regions and Moscow for this election.
AP reports United Russia is expected to retain overwhelming control of the Duma; this is a forecast, not an official result.

story_report.summary: Russia began three days of voting on September 18 in its first parliamentary election during wartime, with all 450 State Duma seats at stake. The contest features virtually no opposition: Yabloko has been removed from the party-list ballot, while the other nine registered parties support President Vladimir Putin’s policies. United Russia is expected to retain overwhelming control of the Duma, although voting remains under way and no official results have been established.

sections.heading: Yabloko’s Ballot Exclusion
sections.body: Russia’s Supreme Court cancelled Yabloko’s federal list registration on August 10, and an appellate ruling on August 17 left the decision intact. The court said the case involved alleged copyright violations in campaign material and funds received from people who had themselves received foreign-state financing; it said extremism allegations were outside the case. Yabloko co-founder Grigory Yavlinsky described the exclusion as a refusal to engage people raising uncomfortable questions and said the party sought peace, freedom and life without fear. The party still has candidates in single-seat races.

sections.heading: Voting in Occupied Ukrainian Territories
sections.body: For the first time in a Russian parliamentary election, the electorate includes residents of four Ukrainian regions seized by Russia after 2022; voting is also taking place in Crimea. Russia’s Central Election Commission adopted special rules for the Duma vote under martial law in parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry says the voting in temporarily occupied territory is illegal and void and that it will not recognize resulting commissions, mandates or results. Ukraine’s sanctions-policy commissioner has said organizers would face sanctions.

sections.heading: Duma Vote Procedures
sections.body: The Central Election Commission scheduled voting for September 18, 19 and 20, with special early-day arrangements for some remote locations and voters abroad. Voters cast two ballots to fill 225 seats from party lists and 225 in single-member constituencies. The commission also authorized remote electronic voting in specified regions and Moscow.

unresolved.text: The effect of Yabloko’s remaining single-seat candidacies cannot be assessed until district results are reported.
The packet does not establish turnout, final seat totals, certified-result timing, the number of votes cast in occupied territory, or whether new sanctions will be imposed.

related_stories.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has ordered protective measures for the country's critical infrastructure and defense industry in response to escalating Russian hybrid attacks. This announcement followed a meeting with political party leaders to discuss the growing threats from Russia, particularly in light of recent developments in Europe. Macron emphasized that the hybrid threat from Moscow has intensified in recent weeks, necessitating immediate action.

related_stories.title: Trump Threatens Kennedy Center Demolition Amid Legal Ruling
related_stories.summary: President Trump stated that the Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' if he does not receive 'recognition.' This comment follows a federal judge's ruling that requires the Trump administration to provide 30 days' notice before making any major changes, including demolition, to the Kennedy Center. The judge's order comes after the center's board, aligned with Trump, faced restrictions on adding a tribute to him.
